title: What Solomon Got Wrong About Love
paragraphs:
What Solomon Got Wrong About Love
The King Who Had Everything… Except What Mattered Most

There is something unsettling about a man who had everything the world could offer… and still wrote, “Meaningless, meaningless… everything is meaningless” (הֲבֵל הֲבָלִים — hevel havalim, Ecclesiastes 1:2). Not a poor man. Not a broken man in the eyes of society. A king. A legend. A man gifted with wisdom directly from God.
Solomon.

The one who spoke in proverbs that still echo across centuries. The one who built the Temple of the Lord. The one who had riches beyond imagination, influence beyond politics, and access to anything his heart desired.
And yet… when it came to love, Solomon got something deeply, painfully wrong.
Because love was never supposed to be something you collect.
It was supposed to be something you surrender into.
Solomon didn’t just love once. He multiplied love into numbers, into status, into possession. Scripture doesn’t hide it. It exposes it.
“He had 700 wives, princesses, and 300 concubines” (1 Kings 11:3).
Seven hundred.
Three hundred.
One thousand relationships… and still not one that anchored his soul to God.

In Hebrew, the word often used for love is אַהֲבָה (ahavah) — a word that implies devotion, covenant, giving, and deep relational commitment. But Solomon drifted from ahavah into something else… something hollow.
Desire without devotion.
Connection without covenant.
Presence without purity.
And slowly, almost quietly, love turned into distraction… and distraction turned into compromise.
“His wives turned away his heart after other gods” (1 Kings 11:4).
Read that again.
Not his enemies.
Not war.
Not poverty.
Love… misaligned… turned his heart away from God.
That’s the part we don’t talk about enough.
Because it feels too close to home.
We live in a world that tells us love is about finding someone who makes us feel complete. Someone who fills the emptiness. Someone who gives us what we think we lack.
But Solomon tried that.
A thousand times.
And still ended up empty.
Because love without God at the centre doesn’t complete you… it consumes you.

The Greek word often used in the New Testament for divine love is ἀγάπη (agapē) — selfless, sacrificial, God-rooted love. It’s not based on emotion alone. It’s anchored in truth, obedience, and holiness.
That’s the love Solomon slowly walked away from.
And if you’re honest… some of us are walking that same road right now.
You don’t need a thousand relationships to lose your heart.
Sometimes it only takes one.
One person who pulls you away from prayer.
One attachment that replaces your hunger for God.
One compromise you keep justifying because it “feels right.”
And suddenly, your spirit feels distant… but you can’t explain why.
Solomon didn’t fall overnight.
He drifted.
And drifting is dangerous because it feels normal while it’s happening.
You still look okay on the outside.
You still function.
You still smile.
But internally… something is slowly disconnecting.
That’s why Ecclesiastes feels so heavy. It’s not just philosophy.
It’s regret.
It’s the voice of a man who realized too late that he chased everything… except the only thing that could have truly satisfied him.
“I denied myself nothing my eyes desired… yet when I surveyed all that my hands had done… everything was meaningless” (Ecclesiastes 2:10–11).
Imagine having everything… and still feeling nothing.
That’s what happens when love is built on anything other than God.
And yet… this is where the Gospel steps in.
Because the story doesn’t end with Solomon’s failure.
It points us to Someone greater.
Jesus.
Where Solomon had divided love, Jesus had undivided devotion.
Where Solomon was surrounded by many but spiritually empty, Jesus was rejected by many but completely fulfilled in the Father.
Where Solomon’s love led him away from God, Jesus’ love led Him to the cross.
“Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one’s life for one’s friends” (John 15:13).
That is agapē.
That is love done right.
And here’s the part that changes everything…
Jesus doesn’t just show us what love is.
He restores what we’ve broken.
So if you’ve been loving the wrong way…
If your heart has been divided…
If something — or someone — has quietly taken God’s place…
You are not too far gone.
But you do have to be honest.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected, didn’t it?
You’re not alone in this.
There are people reading this right now who feel exactly what you feel.
And your honesty might be the thing that helps them come back too.
Don’t keep this to yourself.
And if this spoke to you deeply… stay close.
If your heart is ready to stop drifting… and start returning…
This is your moment.
Because at the end of everything Solomon chased… the truth remained painfully simple:
Without God, even love becomes empty.
But with Jesus… even your broken love can be redeemed.
And the most dangerous thing isn’t losing love…
It’s loving anything more than Him.
